Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the inner workings of the Google Ads auction algorithm (retrieval, elimination, ranking, and auction pricing) alongside advanced catalog expansion techniques ("surface area scaling") and simplified Performance Max configuration for e-commerce. modules: [ADC] topics: [algorithm mechanics, return on ad spend (ROAS), campaign setup and tracking] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. algorithm mechanics / Decoding Google Ads' internal four-step ranking process: retrieval (matching relevant ads), elimination (discarding non-viable entries based on the DOJ-disclosed ad score formula involving bids, predicted click-through rates [PCTR], and quality/experience penalties), ranking (ordering ads by ad score), and the auction (calculating dynamic cost-per-click [CPC] based on buyer intent and advertiser relevance). campaign setup and tracking / Structuring lean Performance Max (PMax) campaigns for e-commerce by removing distracting secondary placements (Gmail, Display, Maps, Discover) and focusing budget heavily on high-intent search and shopping. Leveraging automated bidding strategies like target ROAS (tROAS) or maximize conversion value only after baseline conversion histories are established. return on ad spend (ROAS) / Scaling e-commerce profitability through "surface area scaling"—multiplying product feed variations across diverse price tiers, image angles (targeting distinct buyer avatars), and keyword-stuffed titles. Maximizing impression share in top auction rankings to capture up to 40% of clicks from prime search positions.

Look for. The four core steps of the Google Ads algorithm: retrieval, elimination, ranking, and auction. The definition of "surface area scaling": duplicating product listings across distinct pricing tiers, lifestyle images, and keyword-rich titles to dominate multiple slots in search and shopping results. The formula for the ad score: a blend of bids, predicted click-through rates (PCTR), and a penalty variable (beta) reflecting user experience and landing page quality.
Skip. General personal background stories, college dorm room anecdotes, or vague agency promotional calls to action.
